stem: A 2-year-old girl, weighed in clinic last week at 14 kg, has been brought into the emergency department 12 minutes after biting into a cashew biscuit at a family gathering. She is now floppy in her father's arms. Spreading urticaria covers her face and trunk and her lips are swollen. Brassy inspiratory stridor and audible wheeze are heard at the bedside. She has no prior cardiorespiratory disease and no documented allergy history. Intravenous access has been attempted once unsuccessfully.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 175/min, blood pressure 75/45 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Floppy but rousable; widespread urticaria, lip swelling, stridor, wheeze; capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.8 mmol/L; tryptase to send after stabilisation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate adrenaline dose and route to give first?

options.text: Adrenaline 300 micrograms intramuscularly into the deltoid muscle of the right upper arm.
options.rationale: 300 mcg is the ASCIA dose for children over 20 kg, and deltoid is not the recommended IM site for paediatric anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Adrenaline 140 micrograms calculated as 10 mcg/kg intramuscularly into the lateral thigh.
options.rationale: ASCIA uses banded weight-based dosing for IM adrenaline rather than mg/kg arithmetic to avoid calculation errors in a crisis. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Adrenaline 150 micrograms intramuscularly into the anterolateral mid-thigh muscle.
options.rationale: ASCIA bands by weight: 10 to 20 kg receives 150 mcg IM into the anterolateral thigh as first dose. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Adrenaline 14 micrograms (1 mcg/kg) intravenously after gaining rapid intraosseous access.
options.rationale: IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis with cardiac monitoring and experienced staff; IM is the first dose. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 via nebuliser to manage the stridor while obtaining IV access.
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline can help upper airway oedema as an adjunct but does not replace IM adrenaline as first-line treatment. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

explanation.summary: ASCIA bands IM adrenaline dosing by approximate weight to remove arithmetic errors during an acute event. A child of 10 to 20 kg gets 150 mcg IM (the EpiPen Jr equivalent dose), 20 kg and above gets 300 mcg, and 50 kg and above gets 500 mcg. The IM site is the anterolateral mid-thigh, which delivers reliable absorption even in shock. IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory cases under monitoring.
key_points: 10 to 20 kg = 150 mcg IM adrenaline.
Anterolateral mid-thigh is the only recommended IM site in paediatric anaphylaxis.
Repeat IM adrenaline every 5 minutes until clinical response or commencement of adrenaline infusion.
explanation.pearls: If you cannot recall the band, an EpiPen Jr 150 mcg auto-injector is the right device for any child clearly in the 10 to 20 kg range; deploy it and call for help.

stem:
A 2-year-old presents at midnight with a 1-day history of coryza and a barking cough that has progressively worsened. His mother says his voice is hoarse and that he sounds 'noisy when he breathes in', even when he is sitting still on her lap. He is not drooling. He is fully immunised.

On arrival he is sitting upright on his mother, alert and quietly tearful. You can hear intermittent inspiratory stridor at rest. There is mild chest-wall in-drawing but no tracheal tug, and no cyanosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 97% in air, temperature 37.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Sitting comfortably, inspiratory stridor at rest, mild intercostal recession only, no tracheal tug, no cyanosis, voice hoarse

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Observation without medication for 30 minutes, then reassess severity
options.rationale: Once stridor is present at rest with any work of breathing, AU paediatric guidance gives a single dose of dexamethasone immediately; the benefit at 30 minutes is unlikely to occur without treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup laryngotracheobronchitis)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.60 mg/kg as a single dose, then reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup (marked distress, exhaustion, cyanosis or impaired consciousness); using it for moderate croup over-treats and increases hyperglycaemia and behavioural side effects without added benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup laryngotracheobronchitis)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL alone, without any corticosteroid
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is added for severe croup but is short-acting and rebounds; AU practice always pairs it with corticosteroid, never replaces steroid with adrenaline. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup laryngotracheobronchitis)

options.text: Inhaled budesonide 2 mg via nebuliser, without any oral corticosteroid
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is reserved for children who cannot tolerate oral dexamethasone (vomiting or refusing); oral dexamethasone is the AU first-line because it works equally and is simpler. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup laryngotracheobronchitis)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose, then reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: RCH grades this presentation as moderate croup (stridor at rest, mild work of breathing, no severe distress), and the recommended dose is oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg; the higher 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup laryngotracheobronchitis)

explanation.summary: Croup is parainfluenza-driven viral laryngotracheobronchitis with peak incidence in 6 months to 6 years. RCH grades severity by stridor and work of breathing: mild (no stridor at rest, mild barking cough), moderate (stridor at rest with mild-moderate retractions, no marked distress), and severe (marked distress, exhaustion, cyanosis, decreased conscious state). Mild and moderate croup are treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg; severe gets 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 and a minimum 3-hour observation after the last adrenaline dose.
key_points: Mild/moderate croup: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose.
Severe croup: oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PLUS nebulised adrenaline 5 mL 1:1000 (flat dose).
Observation 3 hours minimum after last nebulised adrenaline for rebound.
Nebulised budesonide is the backup for children who cannot tolerate oral dose.
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild-to-moderate, 0.6 mg/kg only when severe; nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1:1000.

stem:
An 8-month-old boy on day 4 of RSV bronchiolitis was started on low-flow nasal-prong oxygen at 2 L/min two hours ago after his SpO2 dropped to 88% in room air. Despite this he has worsening intercostal and subcostal recessions and is now too tired to feed.

He was born at 38 weeks with no chronic lung disease or congenital cardiac disease. He has had no apnoeas. A repeat capillary blood gas has just returned.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 72, SpO2 91% on 2 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 37.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Marked recessions and tracheal tug, head bobbing, scattered crackles and wheeze, alert but exhausted
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.31, pCO2 56 mmHg, HCO3 25 mmol/L, base excess -1; chest X-ray hyperinflation without consolidation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next respiratory support step?

options.text: Add nebulised hypertonic saline 3% three times daily
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not recommended in the RCH pathway because randomised data show no consistent reduction in length of stay or admission rates, and it may worsen bronchospasm. It does not address impending respiratory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Proceed to elective intubation and conventional mechanical ventilation
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for failure of non-invasive escalation (HFNC then CPAP), apnoeas requiring repeated stimulation, or refractory hypoxaemia. He should first be offered HFNC because most infants respond. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Escalate to heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis pathway reserves HFNC for infants who fail a trial of low-flow oxygen, defined by ongoing distress or rising pCO2 after 1 to 2 hours. He has now had a fair trial of low-flow with rising work of breathing, hypoxia despite 2 L/min, and a pCO2 of 56 with feeding failure - this meets the escalation criterion. HFNC at 2 L/kg/min is the next step before CPAP or intubation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and ipratropium 250 micrograms
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended in infants under 12 months with bronchiolitis because randomised data show no benefit and adverse effects of tachycardia and tremor. The pathophysiology is mucus plugging and airway oedema, not bronchospasm. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Continue low-flow oxygen at 2 L/min and reassess in a further 2 hours
options.rationale: Continuing low-flow misses the failure-of-low-flow criterion (rising pCO2, feeding inability, recessions despite 2 L/min) and risks decompensation. RCH explicitly defines this as the trigger to escalate. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: RCH bronchiolitis pathway makes low-flow nasal-prong oxygen the first step (target SpO2 above 90%) and reserves HFNC for failure of low-flow after about 1 to 2 hours. Rising pCO2, ongoing distress, and feeding inability define failure. HFNC is set at 2 L/kg/min for the first 10 kg.
key_points: Low-flow first, HFNC second, CPAP third in the RCH bronchiolitis pathway
Failure-of-low-flow criteria: rising pCO2, persistent recessions, feeding inability, SpO2 below 90% despite oxygen
Bronchodilators, steroids, hypertonic saline and chest physiotherapy are NOT routine in infant bronchiolitis
explanation.pearls: Target SpO2 in RCH is 90% or above, not 92 to 94% (the higher target leads to longer admissions without outcome benefit). HFNC weight-based flow is capped at 2 L/kg/min up to 10 kg, then 50 L/min absolute thereafter.

stem:
A 9-year-old girl with known asthma is brought to the paediatric resuscitation bay by ambulance after 6 hours of worsening shortness of breath at home. She normally uses fluticasone 100 mcg twice daily and salbutamol PRN. Her last admission was 18 months ago with a 2-day ward stay.

On arrival paramedics had given continuous nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium and a single oral prednisolone dose. She has had three back-to-back salbutamol/ipratropium nebulisers in the resuscitation bay over the last 20 minutes with minimal change. The paediatric registrar is at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 44, SpO2 90% on 8 L/min via face mask, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Sitting forward, speaking 2-3 word sentences, subcostal recession, widespread expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally, no silent chest, alert and frightened
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.34, pCO2 44 mmHg (rising from 38 on arrival), HCO3 23, lactate 3.2; chest X-ray hyperinflation, no pneumothorax
data_table.Medications: Salbutamol 2.5 mg/ipratropium 250 mcg back-to-back nebulisers x 3, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg given 30 minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to continuous nebulised salbutamol 10 mg/hour for the next hour
options.rationale: Continuous salbutamol provides no benefit over back-to-back dosing once delivery is already maximised; this patient has already failed three back-to-back nebulisers with rising CO2 and lactate. Escalation, not repetition, is needed. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes
options.rationale: RCH severe acute asthma pathway escalates to IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes after failure of inhaled bronchodilators and systemic corticosteroid. Magnesium acts as a smooth muscle relaxant and is the first parenteral agent to add. The rising CO2 and lactate plus reduced air entry indicate severe disease requiring this step. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Commence intravenous aminophylline loading dose 5 mg/kg over 60 minutes
options.rationale: IV aminophylline is reserved for asthma not responding to magnesium AND salbutamol infusion; it is a later-line agent because of its narrow therapeutic index. Magnesium is the next escalation here. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline 10 mcg/kg into the lateral thigh
options.rationale: Intramuscular adrenaline is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, not for acute asthma without anaphylactic features. There is no urticaria, angioedema, or hypotension to suggest anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Intubate and ventilate after rapid-sequence induction with ketamine
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for actual or imminent respiratory arrest (exhaustion, silent chest, coma, or severe acidosis). This child is alert, talking in short sentences and has not yet had IV magnesium - parenteral pharmacotherapy is the next step before intubation. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Severe asthma not responding to inhaled bronchodilators and oral steroid escalates to IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes per the RCH pathway. IV salbutamol infusion (5 mcg/kg/min) is the next addition if magnesium fails. Aminophylline is third-line. Intubation is reserved for true respiratory failure - alert, talking patients are managed pharmacologically first.
key_points: RCH severe asthma escalation order: nebulised salbutamol/ipratropium -> oral steroid -> IV magnesium -> IV salbutamol -> aminophylline
IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes
Intubation reserved for actual or imminent respiratory arrest
explanation.pearls: A rising CO2 from a previously hyperventilating asthmatic is a red flag for fatigue; the venous pCO2 normalising or rising in severe asthma signals decompensation rather than improvement.

stem:
A 14-month-old boy is admitted on day 6 of fever to 39.5 °C unresponsive to paracetamol and ibuprofen. He has been irritable and off feeds. His mother reports a non-pruritic rash that appeared on day 3 and faded, and his lips are now red and cracked. He has not had conjunctival injection or lymphadenopathy noted on previous reviews.

On examination today his lips are red and fissured with a strawberry tongue. There is firm dorsal hand and foot oedema with peeling skin at the fingertips. He has no neck node enlargement and no rash currently. He has been started on empirical IV flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone for possible staphylococcal toxic shock.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162, BP 88/52 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Red fissured lips, strawberry tongue, BCG scar erythema, peripheral oedema and periungual desquamation, no conjunctival injection, no cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (110-140), white cell count 22 x10^9/L (5-15), platelets 740 x10^9/L (150-450), CRP 152 mg/L (<5), ESR 78 mm/h, ALT 88 U/L (<40), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145), urinalysis sterile pyuria
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol, ibuprofen, IV flucloxacillin, IV ceftriaxone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue empirical antibiotics for a further 48 hours before reassessing as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Persistent fever beyond 5 days with mucocutaneous changes and a markedly inflammatory profile should redirect away from staphylococcal toxic shock toward Kawasaki disease. Delay risks coronary artery aneurysm. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Refer for percutaneous coronary angiography to evaluate for coronary involvement
options.rationale: Echocardiography is the first-line imaging for coronary surveillance in Kawasaki disease in children, with high sensitivity for proximal coronary aneurysms. Invasive angiography has no first-line role. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Commence IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse therapy as initial monotherapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are added in IVIG-resistant Kawasaki or risk-stratified primary therapy, but the standard initial treatment is IVIG plus aspirin. Steroid monotherapy is not used at presentation in AU practice. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture to exclude bacterial meningitis before further therapy
options.rationale: LP is not indicated in the absence of meningism, altered consciousness or seizure, and would delay urgent IVIG. Aseptic meningitis can occur in Kawasaki but is a supportive feature, not an indication for LP. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Arrange transthoracic echocardiogram and commence IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with high-dose aspirin
options.rationale: This child meets American Heart Association incomplete Kawasaki criteria (fever ≥5 days plus two principal features - rash and oral changes - plus supportive labs: CRP ≥30, anaemia for age, platelets ≥450, albumin ≤30, ALT elevated, sterile pyuria). Treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours plus aspirin to reduce coronary artery aneurysm risk; echocardiogram baselines coronary anatomy. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when fever lasts at least 5 days with fewer than four classical criteria but supportive laboratory abnormalities (CRP, anaemia, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, transaminitis, sterile pyuria) are present. Treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin, with baseline echocardiography. Delaying treatment past day 10 increases coronary aneurysm risk substantially. Steroids, LP, and angiography are not first-line.
key_points: Fever ≥5 days + 2 features + lab criteria = incomplete KD by AHA
IVIG 2 g/kg + aspirin within first 10 days reduces aneurysm risk
Echocardiogram is the imaging modality of choice
BCG scar erythema is a supportive AU-specific feature
explanation.pearls: Treating Kawasaki within 10 days of fever onset cuts coronary aneurysm rate from about 25% to under 5%. BCG scar erythema is a useful local feature in AU practice.

subtopic_detail: Severe croup combined adrenaline and dexamethasone
stem:
You are the ED registrar in a regional hospital. A 3-year-old girl presents with a 2 day history of barking cough and is now in obvious respiratory distress. Her mother reports she has been getting worse over the last 6 hours and tonight became too agitated to drink. She has no history of atopy or previous intubation. She is not vaccinated for diphtheria.

On arrival she is agitated, sitting forwards, with marked stridor at rest, tracheal tug, and intercostal recession. Her voice is hoarse but she is not drooling. She has received no treatment prior to arrival. Examination otherwise is unremarkable with no facial swelling and no rash.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162/min, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 50/min, SpO2 91% room air, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Agitated, sitting forwards; severe stridor at rest; tracheal tug; intercostal recession; no drooling; oropharynx not inspected to avoid distress
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging performed (would distress and worsen airway); throat swab deferred

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 alone, observe for 30 minutes only
options.rationale: Adrenaline acts within 10-30 minutes but lasts only 2 hours; without concurrent dexamethasone there is rebound after wearing off, so steroids must accompany the adrenaline. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg alone, observe response over 1 hour
options.rationale: The 0.15 mg/kg dose is for mild to moderate croup; severe croup with stridor at rest and recession needs both 0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline together. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 plus oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, observe 3 hours
options.rationale: Severe croup with agitation and stridor at rest mandates combined treatment: nebulised adrenaline as a flat 5 mL of 1:1000 plus a 0.6 mg/kg steroid dose, with a minimum 3 hour post-adrenaline observation to detect rebound. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Immediate gas induction and intubation by the most experienced clinician available
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for failure of medical therapy or impending respiratory arrest; the vast majority of severe croup responds to combined adrenaline and steroid without airway intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Heliox 70:30 by face mask while awaiting paediatric retrieval team
options.rationale: Heliox has limited evidence in croup and is not first-line in any Australian guideline; combined adrenaline and steroid is the priority and works within 30 minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Severe croup is defined by stridor at rest with agitation, marked recession, or hypoxia, and is treated with nebulised adrenaline at a flat dose of 5 mL of 1:1000 (regardless of weight) plus oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg. Observation must continue for at least 3 hours after the last nebulised adrenaline to detect rebound. The candidate must avoid the common error of conflating mild-moderate dosing (0.15 mg/kg) with severe dosing.
key_points: Nebulised adrenaline dose in croup is a flat 5 mL of 1:1000, not weight-based.
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg PO for mild-moderate; 0.6 mg/kg for severe.
Minimum 3 hours observation after last nebulised adrenaline before discharge.
Do not inspect the oropharynx if epiglottitis is on the differential.
explanation.pearls: Severe croup needs both an immediate-acting nebulised adrenaline and a long-acting steroid started together within minutes, not sequentially.

stem:
A 2-year-old girl presents to the emergency department at 23:00 with 36 hours of coryza, fever, and a brassy nocturnal cough. Her parents say she has had stridor only when she gets upset and woke her up tonight.

In triage she is settled on her father's lap. There is occasional inspiratory stridor at rest with mild suprasternal retractions, no drooling, and no tripod posture. She tracks faces and is engaged with the toys offered. Air entry is good bilaterally with no wheeze. She has had one previous mild croup episode aged 18 months that settled with no specific treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: well perfused, mild suprasternal recession, occasional stridor at rest, good air entry both sides, no drooling, normal voice with brassy cough, normal mental state
data_table.Investigations: clinical diagnosis, no imaging or bloods indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose with discharge planning after a period of observation
options.rationale: RCH CPG categorises this as moderate croup (stridor at rest with mild recessions, no other severity features). The recommended dose is dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild or moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup. Onset is within 1 to 2 hours, and most moderate cases can be discharged after observation. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single dose with discharge planning after a period of observation
options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg is the dose for severe croup with marked recessions, tracheal tug, agitation or cyanosis. Using it for moderate croup over-treats and adds no incremental clinical benefit; RCH recommends the 0.15 mg/kg dose for mild and moderate disease. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with mandatory 4-hour observation in short-stay unit
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is for severe croup or moderate croup not responding to dexamethasone after 30 minutes of observation. Giving it first-line in a child who is stable with mild recessions exposes her to rebound and obliges unnecessary admission. RCH minimum post-adrenaline observation is 3 hours, not 4. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose with discharge planning after a period of observation
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide has equivalent efficacy to oral dexamethasone in some trials but is more expensive and harder to deliver to an upset toddler. RCH recommends oral dexamethasone as preferred first-line. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Salbutamol 600 micrograms via spacer with 4 puffs every 20 minutes for 1 hour and reassess
options.rationale: Salbutamol treats lower airway bronchospasm, not the subglottic oedema of croup. Stridor that does not change with salbutamol is the textbook finding. Using it here delays effective steroid therapy. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

explanation.summary: Moderate croup in the RCH classification (stridor at rest, mild to moderate recessions, no agitation or cyanosis) is treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg. The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup. Nebulised adrenaline is added if severe or if moderate disease does not respond after 30 minutes of observation following steroid.
key_points: RCH dexamethasone dose is 0.15 mg/kg for mild and moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg only for severe.
Post-nebulised-adrenaline observation is at least 3 hours.
Nebulised adrenaline dose is 5 mL of 1 in 1000 (a flat dose, not weight-based).
Salbutamol has no role in croup.
explanation.pearls: Use dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild and moderate croup per RCH CPG; reserve 0.6 mg/kg for severe disease where adrenaline is also given.
